title: Quantization & Model Optimization
scopeHtml: Scope: Quantization, pruning, distillation and caching techniques that shrink or speed up models.

notes.title: Quantization
notes.html:
What it is. Representing weights (and optionally activations and the KV cache) with fewer bits. Standard training precision is bf16/fp16 (16 bits). Quantization maps them to int8/fp8 (8 bits), 4-bit, or even lower, using a scale (and sometimes zero-point) per tensor, per channel, or per group of weights (e.g. 64 or 128 values per group).

Why it helps.

  • Memory: a 70B model drops from 140 GB (fp16) to 70 GB (int8) or ~35 to 40 GB (4-bit). That can mean fitting on 1 to 2 GPUs instead of 4.
  • Speed: decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so reading fewer bytes per token speeds it roughly in proportion (up to 2 to 3x), provided the kernels dequantize efficiently.
  • Cost: fewer GPUs per replica, more concurrent requests.

What is quantized.

  • Weight-only (W4A16, W8A16): weights stored in low bit, dequantized on the fly to fp16 for compute. Easiest, largest memory savings, small speed gains at large batch.
  • Weight + activation (W8A8, FP8): both low-precision, enabling int8/fp8 tensor-core math for real compute speedups at high batch sizes. Activations contain outliers (a few huge values) that make naive quantization hurt quality; methods like SmoothQuant move the difficulty into the weights.
  • KV-cache quantization (fp8/int8): cuts cache memory in half, extends context/concurrency; check long-context accuracy.

Methods.

  • Post-training quantization (PTQ): quantize a trained model using a small calibration set. GPTQ (layer-wise, second-order error minimization), AWQ (protects the most important "salient" weights found from activation statistics), LLM.int8(), GGUF/llama.cpp quant types (Q8_0, Q5_K_M, Q4_K_M...) for CPU/edge use, bitsandbytes NF4 (used by QLoRA).
  • Quantization-aware training (QAT): simulate low precision during training/fine-tuning so the model adapts; best quality at very low bits but needs training compute.

Quality impact. 8-bit is usually near-lossless. 4-bit weight-only costs a small accuracy drop (often 0.5 to 2 points on benchmarks) but can be larger on hard reasoning, code, maths, long-context recall, rare languages, and precise instruction following. 2 to 3 bits usually degrades noticeably. Larger models tolerate quantization better than small ones. Perplexity is a weak proxy; run your own task eval on the quantized model, including tails and safety/refusal behaviour.

Practical choices.

Need Option
Serve a big model on fewer GPUs AWQ/GPTQ 4-bit or FP8
High throughput on H100/B200 FP8 weights + activations
Run on laptop/phone/CPU GGUF Q4/Q5
Fine-tune a big model on one GPU QLoRA (NF4 base)

Real life. Compressing a photo to JPEG: much smaller, usually indistinguishable, but fine detail can be lost and heavy compression shows artifacts.

Interview angle. Why quantization speeds up decode (memory-bound), why activation outliers are hard, and how you validate a quantized model.

notes.title: Pruning and sparsity
notes.html:
Unstructured pruning. Zero out individual low-magnitude weights (e.g. 50 percent). Easy to achieve with small accuracy loss, but standard GPUs cannot skip zeros efficiently, so there is little speedup unless the hardware/format supports it.

Semi-structured (N:M) sparsity. For every group of M weights keep N (e.g. 2:4). NVIDIA Ampere/Hopper sparse tensor cores accelerate 2:4 patterns by up to ~2x in matrix math. Needs pruning plus fine-tuning to recover quality.

Structured pruning. Remove whole attention heads, FFN neurons, or layers. Gives genuine speedups on any hardware (smaller dense model) but removes capacity; usually requires retraining or distillation to recover (e.g. Minitron-style pruning + distillation).

Methods. Magnitude pruning, SparseGPT/Wanda (one-shot, calibration-based), movement pruning (during fine-tuning).

Trade-offs. Quantization is usually the first, simplest, most reliable optimization; pruning is more specialized. Combining pruning, quantization and distillation can give large compression but compounds quality risk, so evaluate each step.

Real life. Trimming a hedge: remove branches that do not shape it; cut carefully, or it looks wrong and needs regrowth (fine-tuning).

notes.title: Distillation
notes.html:
Definition. Train a student model to reproduce the behaviour of a teacher model. The teacher is typically larger and stronger.

Flavours.

  • Sequence-level / output distillation: generate a large set of teacher responses (optionally with reasoning traces), filter them, and fine-tune the student with supervised learning. Works through any API.
  • Logit (soft-label) distillation: minimize KL divergence between student and teacher token distributions; carries more information per example than hard labels ("dark knowledge"). Requires teacher logits and the same tokenizer.
  • Feature/hidden-state distillation and on-policy distillation (the student generates, the teacher scores/corrects) improve fidelity.
  • Task-specific distillation: a narrow task (classification, extraction, routing, tool-call formatting) distilled into a tiny model: often 10 to 100x cheaper at similar task accuracy.

Pipeline. Define the task and eval → assemble diverse unlabeled prompts from real traffic → generate teacher outputs (with verification/filters) → fine-tune the student → evaluate against teacher and baseline, including hard and rare cases → deploy with the teacher as fallback for low-confidence cases → keep refreshing as the task evolves.

Risks. Students inherit teacher errors and biases; they are weaker on out-of-distribution inputs; synthetic data can lack diversity; terms of service of some providers forbid using outputs to train competing models; evaluation leakage if the same prompts are used for training and testing.

Real life. An apprentice trained by a master until they can do the common jobs alone while the master handles the unusual ones.

notes.title: Caching layers
notes.html:
The principle. The cheapest and fastest token is the one you never recompute. Several layers, from most to least safe:

Layer What is reused Typical savings Risks / rules
Prompt / prefix cache (API or server) KV computations of an identical prefix 50 to 90% of input cost, much lower TTFT needs exact prefix match; put dynamic text last; TTL (e.g. 5 min, 1 h option); minimum length
Embedding cache embedding of identical text avoids embedding calls key by (model version, text hash)
Retrieval cache search results for repeated queries lower latency invalidate on index updates
Exact response cache full response for identical (prompt, params, model, version) 100% for repeats only for deterministic, non-personalized requests; include model/prompt version in key
Semantic cache response for similar queries (embedding match above a threshold) high for FAQ-like traffic wrong hits are silent errors; use strict thresholds, verify with a cheap check, never for personalized or time-sensitive answers
Tool-result cache outputs of idempotent tool calls fewer external calls TTL and invalidation

Design tips. Structure prompts as [static system + tools + reference docs] [dynamic user context] [question] so the static part is cacheable. Track hit rate and savings. Include user/tenant and permission scope in cache keys to avoid cross-user leaks. Set TTLs by data freshness requirements. Consider cache stampede protection for hot keys.

Real life. A shop keeping popular items at the front desk instead of fetching from the warehouse each time, and checking the sell-by date.

notes.title: Choosing optimizations
notes.html:
An ordering that works.

  1. Measure first: profile where tokens, time and money go (per feature, per stage).
  2. Reduce work: trim prompts, limit output length, retrieval instead of stuffing, summarize history.
  3. Reuse work: prompt/prefix caching, response caching where safe.
  4. Right-size the model: smallest model passing your eval; route hard cases to larger ones.
  5. Batch offline work with batch APIs / large batches.
  6. Optimize serving: continuous batching, paged attention, speculative decoding, FP8/4-bit quantization.
  7. Specialize: distil or fine-tune a small model for stable, high-volume tasks.
  8. Hardware / architecture changes last.

Guardrails. Every optimization must pass the quality eval, safety checks and a latency/cost comparison. Track quality-per-dollar rather than cost alone. Keep a rollback path, especially for quantized or distilled models.

Decision example. A summarization endpoint costs $40k/month. Profile: 70% of tokens are a repeated 6k-token style guide. Prompt caching cuts that part's cost ~90%, saving ~$25k with a one-day change and no quality risk. Only then consider a smaller model.

Real life. Fix the leaking tap before you replace the boiler.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Quantization. Store weights (and optionally activations/KV cache) in fewer bits. Decode is memory-bound, so 8-bit/4-bit weights give big memory savings and speedups. PTQ methods: GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF; QAT for best low-bit quality; QLoRA uses NF4. 8-bit is nearly lossless, 4-bit small loss with uneven impact on code/maths/long context; always evaluate on your own tasks.

Pruning. Unstructured sparsity rarely speeds up GPUs; 2:4 semi-structured gives up to ~2x; structured pruning gives real speedups but usually needs retraining/distillation.

Distillation. Train a small student from a large teacher's outputs or logits; best for narrow, high-volume tasks; 10 to 100x cheaper with near-teacher accuracy; check licences and out-of-distribution weakness; keep a fallback.

Caching. Layered: provider/server prefix cache (safest, biggest win), embedding/retrieval/tool caches, exact response cache, and risky semantic cache. Put static content first; include tenant/version in keys; manage TTL and invalidation.

Order of optimization. Measure → reduce tokens → reuse (cache) → right-size/route → batch → serving optimizations → specialize → hardware. Every step is gated by an eval.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Quantization speeds up decode because decode reads weights; fewer bytes means faster steps."
  • "Prefix caching is the first optimization to try: free quality, large savings."
  • "A semantic cache can silently serve wrong answers; set thresholds conservatively."
  • "Measure first; the biggest cost is rarely where you expect."

questions.promptHtml: What is quantization of an LLM, and why would you do it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline check that you know the core trade (bits for quality) and can do the memory arithmetic in your head.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A model is billions of numbers (weights), normally stored in 16 bits each. Quantization stores them in fewer bits, such as 8 or 4, using a scale factor to map back to approximate real values. The model gets 2 to 4 times smaller, so it fits on fewer GPUs and runs cheaper, at the cost of a small, uneven loss in accuracy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A weight is just a float. In fp16/bf16 it takes 2 bytes. Quantization picks a small set of levels (int8 has 256, 4-bit has 16) and a scale so that w ≈ scale * q, where q is a small integer. The scale is kept per tensor, per channel, or per group (for example 64 or 128 weights share one scale); smaller groups track the data better but cost extra metadata.

Memory math: params x bytes per param.

  • 70B at fp16: 70e9 x 2 = 140 GB.
  • 70B at int8: 70 GB. At 4-bit: about 35 GB plus scales, roughly 38 to 40 GB.

Three things can be quantized: weights, activations (the intermediate values at runtime), and the KV cache (the stored attention keys and values for the tokens so far). Weights are easiest and give most of the memory savings.

fp16 weight 0.1234  ->  scale 0.01, q = 12 (int8)  ->  dequant 0.12   (small error)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Counting only weights: you still need KV cache and activation memory on top.
  • Saying "no quality loss". 8-bit is near-lossless, 4-bit is a measurable trade.
  • Forgetting the scale metadata when computing size.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Per-tensor vs per-group scale? → Per-group follows local weight ranges better, which matters a lot at 4-bit, for a small storage overhead.
  2. Does it make training cheaper? → Not by itself; PTQ is applied after training. QLoRA uses a 4-bit base to make fine-tuning fit.
  3. Is a 4-bit 70B better than a 16-bit 13B? → Often yes on quality, since bigger models tolerate quantization well, but verify on your task.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "smaller model, a bit less accurate." Senior: does the byte math, separates weights/activations/KV, names granularity, and insists on a task eval.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team sized a deployment from weights only and OOMed under load because KV cache for 40 concurrent 8k-token chats needed more memory than the savings gave back.

questions.promptHtml: Why does 4-bit weight quantization make token generation faster, even though the GPU still computes in fp16?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, a foundational serving idea.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Generating one token means reading every weight from GPU memory once, but doing very little math per weight. So speed is limited by how many bytes you move, not by arithmetic. Storing weights in 4 bits moves a quarter of the bytes, and a fast kernel dequantizes them on the fly in registers, so each step gets close to proportionally faster.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decode produces one token per step per sequence. With batch size 1 the work is a matrix-vector multiply: each weight is loaded and used about once. A GPU can do far more math per second than it can read bytes per second, so the memory read is the bottleneck. Rough ceiling: tokens/s is about bandwidth / bytes of weights read per token.

Example: an 8B model in fp16 is 16 GB. At 1,000 GB/s bandwidth the ceiling is about 62 tokens/s. In 4-bit it is about 4.5 GB, so a ceiling near 200 tokens/s in theory; real gains are 2 to 3x because of dequantization cost, scales, and attention/KV reads that did not shrink.

At large batch sizes the work becomes compute-bound (many sequences reuse each loaded weight), so weight-only quantization helps less; you then need weight plus activation quantization (W8A8/FP8) to use faster low-precision tensor cores.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
params, gbps = 8e9, 1000
for name, bytes_per in [("fp16", 2.0), ("int8", 1.0), ("4bit", 0.5625)]:  # 4bit incl. scales
    print(name, round(gbps * 1e9 / (params * bytes_per), 1), "tok/s ceiling (batch 1)")
fun main() {
    val params = 8e9; val bw = 1000e9
    listOf("fp16" to 2.0, "int8" to 1.0, "4bit" to 0.5625).forEach { (n, b) ->
        println("$n ${"%.1f".format(bw / (params * b))} tok/s ceiling (batch 1)")
    }
}
public class Ceiling {
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        double params = 8e9, bw = 1000e9;
        String[] n = {"fp16", "int8", "4bit"};
        double[] b = {2.0, 1.0, 0.5625};
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
            System.out.printf("%s %.1f tok/s ceiling (batch 1)%n", n[i], bw / (params * b[i]));
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying quantization speeds up "the math". For weight-only it mostly saves bytes moved.
  • Expecting the same gain at batch 64, where the GPU is compute-bound.
  • Ignoring that a slow dequant kernel can erase the gain.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it help prefill? → Little; prefill is compute-bound (many tokens at once).
  2. Why is real speedup below the ceiling? → Dequant overhead, scale reads, KV-cache reads, kernel launch costs.
  3. When would you add activation quantization? → High batch, throughput-focused serving on hardware with fp8/int8 tensor cores.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "fewer bits is faster." Senior: bandwidth-ceiling arithmetic, the batch-size crossover to compute-bound, and the kernel-quality caveat.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An AWQ model gave 2.4x decode at batch 1 on a chat tier but only 1.1x on an overnight batch job at batch 128, which needed FP8 instead.

questions.promptHtml: What is model distillation and when is it a better choice than just using a smaller off-the-shelf model?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you can explain teacher/student and know it is for narrow, high-volume tasks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Distillation trains a small student model to imitate a larger teacher. You run the teacher on many real prompts, keep its good outputs, and fine-tune the student on them. It beats a generic small model when the task is narrow and stable, volume is high, and you can measure quality, because the student becomes specialized and can be 10 to 100x cheaper.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A small off-the-shelf model is general and often weaker on your exact format or domain. A distilled student sees thousands of teacher answers for your task, so it learns your output style, labels and edge cases.

Two main forms: output (sequence-level) distillation trains on the teacher's text answers, which works even through an API; logit distillation matches the teacher's token probability distributions, richer but requires access to teacher logits and the same tokenizer.

Pipeline: define task and eval, sample diverse real prompts, generate and filter teacher outputs, fine-tune, compare against teacher and baseline, deploy with teacher fallback for low-confidence cases.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Distilling a task that changes weekly; the student goes stale.
  • Testing on prompts that were in the training set.
  • Ignoring provider terms that restrict training on their outputs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why "dark knowledge"? → Soft probabilities show which wrong answers are nearly right, more signal than a hard label.
  2. Does the student exceed the teacher? → Rarely on the task overall; it can match it on a narrow distribution.
  3. What if the student is unsure? → Route to the teacher by confidence.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "train small from big." Senior: picks the distillation flavour for the access available, builds a held-out eval, plans the fallback and checks licences.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A ticket-routing classifier distilled from a large model cut cost per call by roughly 50x with accuracy within 1 point on the held-out set.

questions.promptHtml: What is prompt (prefix) caching, and how do you structure a prompt to benefit from it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the cheapest large win in LLM cost work, and the structure rule is a common practical test.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When many requests start with the same long text (system prompt, tool definitions, reference documents), the provider can reuse the already-computed attention state for that prefix instead of recomputing it. Cached input tokens cost much less and the first token arrives sooner. To benefit, put static content first and dynamic content last, because the match must be an exact prefix.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Processing a prompt builds a KV cache (the keys and values each token produces for attention). If the next request begins with identical tokens, that part is reused. Any change at token N invalidates everything after N.

Layout: [system + tools + reference docs] [conversation so far] [new question]. Caches have a minimum length and a time-to-live (for example minutes, with longer options); verify current numbers in the provider docs. With Anthropic you mark a cache breakpoint with cache_control; some providers cache automatically.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # key from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
r = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=300,
    system=[{"type": "text", "text": STYLE_GUIDE, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
)
print(r.usage)  # check cache_creation_input_tokens / cache_read_input_tokens
// Plain REST via OkHttp (no SDK method names assumed). STYLE_GUIDE and question are JSON-escaped strings.
val body = """{"model":"claude-sonnet-5-5","max_tokens":300,
 "system":[{"type":"text","text":"$STYLE_GUIDE","cache_control":{"type":"ephemeral"}}],
 "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"$question"}]}"""
val req = okhttp3.Request.Builder().url("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages")
    .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
    .header("anthropic-version", "2023-06-01")
    .post(body.toRequestBody("application/json".toMediaType())).build()
// java.net.http REST; the official anthropic-java SDK also exposes cache control (verify in the SDK docs).
var body = "{\"model\":\"claude-sonnet-5-5\",\"max_tokens\":300,"
  + "\"system\":[{\"type\":\"text\",\"text\":\"" + STYLE_GUIDE + "\",\"cache_control\":{\"type\":\"ephemeral\"}}],"
  + "\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"" + question + "\"}]}";
var req = java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder(java.net.URI.create("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"))
  .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
  .header("anthropic-version", "2023-06-01").header("content-type", "application/json")
  .POST(java.net.http.HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting a timestamp or user name at the top of the system prompt, breaking every match.
  • Reordering tool definitions between requests.
  • Not reading the usage fields to confirm hits.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does caching change the answer? → No; it is the same computation, reused.
  2. What if traffic is sparse? → The entry may expire between requests; a longer TTL or keep-warm may cost more than it saves.
  3. Cache and privacy? → Caches are scoped per org/workspace by the provider; check the docs for isolation rules.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "turn on caching." Senior: designs the prompt layout, measures hit rate and TTL fit, and models the write-premium break-even.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Moving a per-user greeting from the top of a 6k-token prompt to the bottom raised hit rate from near 0 to over 90 percent.

questions.promptHtml: Explain weight-only (W4A16) versus weight-and-activation (W8A8/FP8) quantization. Why are activation outliers a problem?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know which variant to choose for latency versus throughput.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Weight-only keeps compute in fp16 and just stores weights small, so it saves memory and speeds up memory-bound decode. W8A8 and FP8 also quantize the activations so the matrix math itself runs on low-precision tensor cores, which helps at high batch. Activations have a few huge outlier values that stretch the scale, so most normal values get crushed into few levels; that is why naive activation quantization hurts quality.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Notation: W4A16 means 4-bit weights, 16-bit activations. Weights are static, so you can study and tune them offline. Activations depend on the input, and certain hidden channels in LLMs carry values 10 to 100x larger than the rest. One scale for the whole tensor is set by the outlier, so typical values round to nearly the same few integers.

Remedies: SmoothQuant rescales channels, shifting difficulty from activations into weights (which tolerate it); per-token/per-channel scales; mixed precision keeping outlier channels in fp16 (LLM.int8()); FP8's wider dynamic range handles outliers better than int8.

Variant Saves memory Speeds compute Quality risk Best for
W4A16 most little at big batch low to medium latency, few GPUs
W8A8 / FP8 2x yes, high batch low (FP8) to medium (int8) throughput serving

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing W4A16 for a high-batch offline job and expecting a big throughput gain.
  • Calibrating activation scales on unrepresentative data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not quantize activations per tensor? → Outliers set the scale; use per-token scales.
  2. What is the calibration set for? → To measure activation ranges so scales fit real inputs.
  3. Why FP8 over int8? → Floating point has built-in dynamic range, tolerating outliers better.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "A is activations." Senior: ties the variant to latency vs throughput regime and explains outlier handling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A W8A8 int8 deployment lost several points on code tasks until outlier smoothing was applied and calibration data included code prompts.

questions.promptHtml: Compare GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF quants and bitsandbytes NF4, and say when you would use quantization-aware training instead.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests practical tool knowledge: which method for which deployment target.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: GPTQ and AWQ are post-training methods for GPU serving at 4-bit: GPTQ minimizes layer-wise error using second-order information, AWQ protects the most important weights found from activation statistics. GGUF is the llama.cpp format for CPU and edge with many quant types such as Q4_K_M. NF4 from bitsandbytes is mainly for QLoRA fine-tuning. QAT trains with simulated low precision and is for when PTQ quality is not enough, usually at very low bits.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• PTQ needs a small calibration set (hundreds of samples) and minutes to hours. No training.
  • GPTQ: quantizes layer by layer, adjusting remaining weights to compensate for rounding error.
  • AWQ: finds the roughly 1 percent of weight channels that matter most (because large activations feed them), scales them before quantizing so they lose less precision.
  • GGUF: a file format plus block-wise quant types (Q8_0, Q5_K_M, Q4_K_M) with good CPU kernels and Apple Silicon support.
  • NF4: a 4-bit data type tuned for normally distributed weights, paired with double quantization of scales; the base for QLoRA.
  • QAT: forward pass uses fake-quantized weights, so training adapts. It costs training compute and data.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using NF4 as a production serving format; kernels are slower than AWQ/GPTQ servers.
  • Calibrating on English wikipedia then serving code or another language.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Q4_K_M, what does K mean? → k-quant: block-wise scales with mixed precision across tensors.
  2. Why can a quantized checkpoint on Hugging Face be risky? → Unknown calibration and quality; evaluate it.
  3. When QAT? → 2 to 3 bit targets, small models, or strict accuracy budgets you own the training pipeline for.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "AWQ is better." Senior: maps method to target hardware, knows calibration pitfalls, and treats QAT as the quality escape hatch.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team shipped a community GPTQ checkpoint calibrated on English prose; multilingual support tickets regressed 6 points before they re-quantized with in-domain data.

questions.promptHtml: Explain unstructured, 2:4 semi-structured, and structured pruning. Which one actually makes inference faster?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates assume zeros mean speed. This checks hardware awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Pruning removes weights. Unstructured pruning zeros individual weights, so compression is easy but normal GPUs still multiply the zeros and gain little. 2:4 sparsity keeps 2 of every 4 weights in a pattern NVIDIA sparse tensor cores accelerate, up to roughly 2x on the matrix math. Structured pruning removes whole heads, neurons or layers, giving a smaller dense model that is faster everywhere but loses capacity and usually needs retraining.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Speed needs regular patterns the hardware can exploit. Unstructured sparse matrices have irregular memory access that dense GPU kernels cannot skip. 2:4 is regular, so the chip stores only the kept values plus small index metadata. Structured pruning changes shapes (fewer heads, narrower FFN), so every standard kernel just does less work.

Methods: magnitude pruning, SparseGPT and Wanda (one-shot, calibration-based, no retraining), movement pruning during fine-tuning. Structured pruning is typically followed by distillation from the original model to recover quality.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reporting "50 percent sparse" as a speedup.
  • Skipping the recovery fine-tune after structured pruning.
  • Forgetting that decode is memory-bound, so 2:4 gains in matmul do not translate directly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is pruning less popular than quantization? → Quantization is simpler, more reliable and better supported in serving stacks.
  2. Can you combine them? → Yes, but quality risks compound; evaluate each step.
  3. Which layers prune worst? → Often early and late layers and attention outputs; sensitivity analysis decides.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "remove unimportant weights." Senior: ties each type to hardware support and recovery cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 50 percent unstructured-pruned model held quality but ran at the same latency on A100s, so the project switched to structured pruning plus distillation.

questions.contextHtml: You must serve a 70B-parameter chat model. Budget allows 2 x 80 GB GPUs per replica. Traffic: 30 concurrent users, average 3k tokens of context each. The base model is bf16. A colleague says "just use 4-bit, it will fit." Another says "int8 is safer." The model uses grouped-query attention, and the KV cache costs about 0.3 MB per token in bf16 (assume this figure for the exercise).
questions.promptHtml: Which precision do you pick for weights and KV cache, and show the memory math.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks 4-bit because it is smallest, or computes only the weights. Ignores KV cache and runtime overhead, and does not mention evaluation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Latency target and tail? Quality bar on code or reasoning? Peak concurrency, not average? Is context length growing? Are we on H100-class hardware that supports FP8?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I would start with the budget table.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) bf16 does not fit; (b) int8/FP8 fits with margin; (c) 4-bit fits easily with large headroom; (d) KV cache is the hidden term.
  4. How I'd verify each: Weights bf16: 70e9 x 2 = 140 GB, and 160 GB total leaves 20 GB, but KV for 30 x 3k = 90k tokens x 0.3 MB = 27 GB, so bf16 fails. Int8/FP8: 70 GB weights + 27 GB KV = 97 GB of 160 GB, comfortable. 4-bit: about 38 GB + 27 GB = 65 GB, so it could even fit one GPU at lower concurrency. Add 10 to 15 percent for activations and fragmentation.
  5. Root cause: The real constraint is weights plus KV cache, not weights alone.
  6. Fix: Start with FP8 or int8 weights (near-lossless) and fp16 KV. If concurrency doubles, quantize KV to fp8 (saves about 13 GB at current load) before dropping weights to 4-bit. Run my task eval on each candidate before choosing.
  7. Prevention: Capacity model in the repo, load test at peak, alert on KV utilization.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not pick 4-bit by default: it saves memory we do not need and adds quality risk on code and reasoning. I would not skip the eval because "int8 is safe".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Context grows to 16k per user? → KV becomes 30 x 16k x 0.3 MB = 144 GB; need KV quantization, fewer concurrent users, or more GPUs.
  • Latency matters more than throughput? → 4-bit weight-only can cut decode latency; test it.
  • Hardware is A100 (no FP8)? → Use int8 weights (W8A16) or AWQ 4-bit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team chose 4-bit for "fit" and later found their 8-bit option fit with 40 percent headroom; the 4-bit version lost points on structured-output tasks that nobody had tested.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: weights-only math, no KV cache, no eval.
  • Hire: full budget with KV, picks 8-bit, mentions eval.
  • Strong hire: sizes for peak and growth, sequences KV quantization before 4-bit weights, names hardware dependence.

questions.promptHtml: What caching layers exist in an LLM application, which are safest, and what must go into a response-cache key?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cache bugs are silent correctness and privacy bugs. Interviewers look for a layered mental model and a key design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: From safest to riskiest: provider prefix cache, embedding and retrieval caches, tool-result caches, exact response cache, and semantic cache. The response-cache key must include everything that can change the answer: normalized prompt, model and version, system prompt version, sampling params, tools, and the tenant or user and permission scope. Anything personalized or time-sensitive should not be cached.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Prefix cache reuses computation and never changes output. Embedding cache keys on (embedding model version, text hash). Retrieval cache must be invalidated when the index updates. Exact response cache only makes sense when sampling is deterministic enough (temperature 0 or acceptable variation) and the answer is not user-specific. Semantic cache matches by embedding similarity, so a threshold error returns a wrong but fluent answer.

Operational concerns: TTL by data freshness, stampede protection for hot keys (one request recomputes, others wait), metrics for hit rate and saved cost, a way to purge by model or prompt version.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Key without tenant or user scope, leaking one customer's answer to another.
  • Not versioning the key by prompt or model, serving stale behavior after a deploy.
  • Caching answers that depend on live data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Cache at temperature 0.7? → Same prompt gives varied answers; caching freezes one, which may be fine or not.
  2. Stampede? → Single-flight lock or request coalescing.
  3. How to measure benefit? → Hit rate x cost saved minus lookup cost, plus error rate from bad hits.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cache by prompt string." Senior: scopes by tenant, versions the key, and ranks layers by risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A multi-tenant assistant cached by prompt text only; one customer's pricing answer appeared for another until tenant ID joined the key.

questions.contextHtml:
A support bot sends about 7,000 input tokens per request: a 6,000-token policy manual plus about 1,000 tokens of conversation. Requests per day: 200k. Cache is enabled, yet the dashboard shows a hit rate of 3 percent and the bill is unchanged. Code:

system = f"Current time: {datetime.now().isoformat()}\nUser: {user_name}\n{POLICY_MANUAL}"
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=400,
    system=[{"type": "text", "text": system, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],
    messages=history,
)
questions.promptHtml: Why is the hit rate so low, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the TTL or the provider, or raises the cache size. Misses that the prefix changes on every call.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the manual identical across users? Does the tool list change order? What is the traffic gap per user (TTL fit)? What does the usage object show for cache reads vs writes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the timestamp and user name out of the cached block today; the manual is the prefix worth caching.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) timestamp at the very start changes every request; (b) user name makes the text unique per user; (c) TTL expiry on sparse traffic; (d) below minimum cacheable length (not here, 6k is enough).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens per request; diff two consecutive system prompts for byte equality; compute inter-request gaps.
  5. Root cause: Prefix matching is exact. The first token of difference (the timestamp) invalidates everything after it, so each request writes a new cache entry and never reads one.
  6. Fix:
system = [{"type": "text", "text": POLICY_MANUAL, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}]
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": f"[time {now} | user {user_name}]\n{question}"}]
// Same idea: static manual block first with cache_control; volatile text goes in the user message.
val system = listOf(mapOf("type" to "text", "text" to POLICY_MANUAL, "cache_control" to mapOf("type" to "ephemeral")))
val userMsg = "[time $now | user $userName]\n$question"
// Same idea: static manual block first with cache_control; volatile text goes in the user message.
var userMsg = "[time " + now + " | user " + userName + "]\n" + question;
// system block = POLICY_MANUAL only, marked with cache_control (verify field names in the SDK docs)
  1. Prevention: Unit test that the system prompt is byte-identical across two calls; alert on hit rate below 70 percent; code review rule: no dynamic data before static data.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not shrink the manual first; caching gives most of the saving with no quality risk. Cache writes usually cost a premium, so for very sparse traffic compute the break-even before enabling it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Conversation history grows each turn; cache that too? → Add a second breakpoint at the end of history so earlier turns are reused.
  • Two policy manual versions? → Separate prefixes; roll out gradually to avoid a cold-cache spike.
  • Traffic per user is 1 request per 20 minutes? → TTL may expire; share the manual prefix across users since it is user-independent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "request id for tracing" in the first line of a prompt silently disabled caching for a month; the invoice was the alert.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames infra or TTL only.
  • Hire: finds the timestamp and fixes ordering.
  • Strong hire: also checks usage fields, adds a regression test and breakpoint strategy, and models write premium.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between sequence-level (output) distillation and logit distillation, and which do you use when the teacher is behind an API?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests practical constraints: what access you have decides the method.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Output distillation fine-tunes the student on text the teacher generated; it works through any API. Logit distillation trains the student to match the teacher's full probability distribution over tokens with a KL-divergence loss, which carries more information per example but needs logits and a shared tokenizer. With an API teacher I use output distillation, optionally with reasoning traces, filtered for quality.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
In output distillation each example is a hard target: one sampled answer. In logit distillation each position gives the teacher's whole distribution, so the student learns which alternatives are plausible. This helps when data is small. On-policy distillation lets the student generate and the teacher score or correct it, reducing the train/inference mismatch.

Quality levers with API teachers: diverse prompts from real traffic, rejection sampling or verifier filtering, multiple samples per prompt, and mixing in some human-labeled data.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Training on unfiltered teacher mistakes.
  • Using the same prompts for training and evaluation.
  • Narrow prompt diversity, leading to a brittle student.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why same tokenizer for logit distillation? → Distributions must align token for token.
  2. Temperature in KL distillation? → Higher temperature softens distributions to expose relative probabilities.
  3. Risk of terms of service? → Some providers forbid training competing models on outputs; check.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "teacher labels, student learns." Senior: picks the method by access, filters, and guards against leakage and licence problems.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A distilled extractor trained on unfiltered teacher outputs reproduced the teacher's date-format errors until a rule-based verifier filtered the data.

questions.contextHtml: You moved a code-assistant model from bf16 to AWQ 4-bit to halve GPU cost. Perplexity on a general text set went from 6.10 to 6.25, and the team declared success. Two weeks later: pass@1 on your internal code benchmark dropped from 62 to 54; JSON tool calls fail schema validation 3.1 percent of the time (was 0.8); prompts over 24k tokens miss facts from the beginning. Latency improved 35 percent.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, and how do you handle it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back" with no diagnosis, or "perplexity is fine so the model is fine".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What calibration data was used? Which layers or group size? Was a task eval run before launch? Is the drop uniform or concentrated in some categories?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route code and tool-call traffic back to the bf16 or 8-bit replica while the diagnosis runs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) calibration set was general prose, not code/JSON; (b) 4-bit hurts exact-token tasks and long-range recall more than average text; (c) a too-large group size; (d) a serving-side bug (different sampling or chat template) as a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the same benchmark on bf16, int8 and 4-bit with identical sampling; compare per-category deltas; check outputs for the same prompts; re-quantize with code/JSON calibration and group size 64 or 32.
  5. Root cause: Perplexity on average text is a weak proxy. The calibration set did not represent code and structured output, and 4-bit errors accumulate on tasks with exact syntax and distant recall.
  6. Fix: Short term: split traffic by task. Long term: recalibrate on in-domain data, try 8-bit/FP8 for the quality-critical path, consider QAT, and add constrained decoding for JSON.
  7. Prevention: A release gate: task eval, tool-call validity, long-context recall and safety checks must pass before any precision change.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not give up quantization wholesale: 8-bit may keep most of the savings. Not trust one global metric.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Business says keep the 35 percent latency gain? → Use 4-bit for chat-only tiers, 8-bit for code.
  • Only long context fails? → Check KV quantization and RoPE scaling settings too.
  • Safety refusals changed? → Include red-team and refusal evals in the gate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A model passed a leaderboard-style suite after quantization and failed customers' unit-test-generation tasks; the missing eval had never included multi-file context.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: relies on perplexity, no diagnosis.
  • Hire: task-level eval, recalibration, routing.
  • Strong hire: separates proxy vs task metrics, release gate, mix of precisions per workload.

questions.promptHtml: What is KV-cache quantization, what does it buy you, and what is the failure mode?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: KV cache is often the binding constraint in serving; senior engineers know it scales differently from weights.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The KV cache holds the keys and values of all previous tokens so attention does not recompute them. It grows with batch size and context length. Storing it in fp8 or int8 instead of fp16 halves its memory, allowing more concurrent users or longer contexts. The risk is accuracy loss in long-context retrieval and in tasks where small attention score errors accumulate, so I test long-context recall specifically.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
KV memory per token is about 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes. For long contexts and many users it can exceed the weights. Weights are a fixed cost; KV is a per-request cost.

Halving the bytes also reduces memory traffic in attention, which speeds decode for long sequences. Errors in keys perturb attention scores (softmax is sensitive), while values average out more gently, so some systems use different precision for K and V. Scales per head or per token help.

Combine with other tools: grouped-query attention reduces kv_heads, paged attention reduces fragmentation, prefix caching shares KV across requests.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing on short prompts only; damage shows at 32k+.
  • Assuming support: it needs engine and kernel support.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not quantize it to 4-bit? → Possible in research; error and kernel support limit production use.
  2. Weights vs KV: which first? → If KV dominates memory at your load, KV first; it is cheaper in quality.
  3. Eviction instead? → Token dropping or sliding window loses information; quantization keeps all tokens at lower precision.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "compress memory." Senior: derives KV per token, knows when it dominates, and tests long-context recall.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: FP8 KV doubled concurrency on a 32k-context summarizer; a needle-in-a-haystack check caught a regression that had been hidden by short-prompt tests.

questions.contextHtml: A semantic cache (embedding match, cosine threshold 0.86) fronts an HR assistant. Hit rate is 41 percent, saving about $18k a month. A user complains: asked "What is my PTO balance if I joined in March?" and received another employee's number. Another: "How many days for parental leave in Germany?" got the UK answer. Cache key is the embedding of the question text only. Responses are stored for 7 days.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose, mitigate, and redesign.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Just raises the threshold to 0.95 and moves on.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which answers include personal data? Is tenant/user in the key? Which query classes are safe to cache? What was the measured false-hit rate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the semantic cache for personalized and jurisdiction-dependent intents; purge the 7-day store; notify security/privacy about the leak.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) key lacks user and permission scope, a privacy bug; (b) the threshold is too loose, so "Germany" and "UK" questions are near neighbors; (c) answers depend on live data with a 7-day TTL; (d) embedding is blind to entities and numbers.
  4. How I'd verify each: Sample hits and label correct/incorrect; compute false-hit rate by threshold; replay the two failing queries and check similarity scores; audit which cached answers contain user data.
  5. Root cause: Similarity says "same topic", not "same answer". Missing scope in the key turned a cache into a cross-user leak.
  6. Fix: Short term: key every entry by tenant, user and permission set, and restrict the semantic cache to non-personalized FAQ intents. Long term: add entity checks (country, plan, dates), verify a hit with a cheap model or rules, tune thresholds on labeled pairs, shorten TTL, and track false-hit rate.
def cache_key(q_emb_bucket, tenant, user_scope, model_ver, prompt_ver):
    return (tenant, user_scope, model_ver, prompt_ver, q_emb_bucket)
data class CacheKey(val tenant: String, val scope: String, val modelVer: String,
                    val promptVer: String, val embBucket: String)
record CacheKey(String tenant, String scope, String modelVer, String promptVer, String embBucket) {}
  1. Prevention: Privacy review of every cache, a labeled evaluation set of near-duplicate pairs, alerts on false-hit audits, canary queries.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on the threshold alone; accept lower hit rate for safety. $18k savings do not justify a data leak.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Threshold 0.95 still gives wrong hits? → Embeddings are weak on negation and entities; add the verification step.
  • Want savings back? → Prefix caching on the HR policy text gives safe savings.
  • Legal asks for deletion of a user's data? → Cache must be purge-able by user key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "similar question" cache served the same refund policy to every region, until a legal escalation showed 12 percent of hits were wrong-region.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks threshold only.
  • Hire: adds scope to key, disables for personal intents.
  • Strong hire: privacy incident handling, labeled false-hit measurement, verification layer, safer alternatives.

questions.promptHtml: Your LLM bill is too high. In what order do you optimize, and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors profile first and take the cheap, safe wins before risky ones.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Measure first, then reduce work (shorter prompts, capped output, retrieval instead of stuffing), then reuse work (prefix and response caching), then right-size or route to smaller models, then batch offline jobs, then serving-level tricks like quantization, and only then specialize with distillation or change hardware. Each step has to pass the quality eval.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The order follows risk and effort: caching a static prefix has zero quality risk and a one-day change; quantization is moderate risk; distillation is a project. The biggest cost is rarely where people think, so I break costs down per feature and per stage: input tokens, output tokens (output usually costs more per token), retries, and wasted calls.

Judge by quality-per-dollar, keep a rollback path, and compare latency as well as cost.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Jumping to a cheaper model without measuring quality.
  • Optimizing the 5 percent feature.
  • Ignoring retries and failed calls.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What gets measured? → Tokens in/out, cost, latency and quality by feature.
  2. When is batch API right? → Non-urgent work; discounts exist, verify current terms.
  3. When do you self-host? → Stable high volume, privacy needs, and when API unit cost exceeds GPU cost at your utilization.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use a smaller model." Senior: profile, order by risk, gate by eval, keep rollback.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team spent weeks on quantization when a 5,000-token boilerplate in every call was 60 percent of spend.

questions.contextHtml: A summarization endpoint costs $40k per month. Profiling shows: 70 percent of input tokens are a repeated 6k-token style guide; average output is 900 tokens against an actual need of about 300; 8 percent of calls are retries from timeouts; p95 latency is 9 s and the product wants under 5 s. Traffic is steady, 24/7, about 2M calls per month. A teammate proposes immediately distilling a smaller model (3-month project).
questions.promptHtml: What is your plan and expected outcome?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Agrees with distillation first, or proposes a vague "use cheaper model".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Current cache status? Quality metric for summaries? Is the style guide identical for all users? How are outputs measured by users? What triggers retries?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cost is not an outage; quick wins first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) caching the style guide cuts most input cost; (b) trimming output to 300 tokens cuts output cost and latency; (c) retries from timeouts waste 8 percent; (d) a smaller model helps only after the above.
  4. How I'd verify each: Enable prefix caching and read cache usage fields; add max_tokens plus an instruction for length; compare summaries with an eval set; trace the timeout cause.
  5. Root cause: Repeated static text is paid at full price, output is padded, and timeouts inflate cost.
  6. Fix: Prefix caching on the style guide: about 70 percent of input at roughly 90 percent discount, potentially saving $25k as in the notes (verify with the real pricing and write premium). Output capping reduces latency since decode time is proportional to output tokens, likely getting p95 under 5 s. Fix timeout/retry policy (8 percent wasted). Re-profile; only if the remainder is still high, evaluate a smaller model or distillation.
  7. Prevention: Per-feature cost dashboard; hit rate and output-length alerts; eval gate on summary quality.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not distill first: three months for gains available in days. Not cut output without checking summaries stay complete.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cache hit rate only 50 percent? → Check prefix stability and TTL, share across users.
  • Quality drops with shorter outputs? → Add a length target and structure rather than a hard cap.
  • Still $15k after all this? → Now consider a smaller model or batch for non-urgent calls.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A project planned a model swap for a 10x saving; a one-line prompt reorder delivered 60 percent of it that week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks distillation or model downgrade first.
  • Hire: caching and output cap, rough savings.
  • Strong hire: full profile-driven plan with latency, retries, eval gate and staged decision for model change.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech routes 4M support messages a month through a large model to classify intent (30 labels) and extract 5 fields as JSON. Cost is $22k a month; accuracy against 3,000 human-labeled messages is 94 percent. Leadership wants costs under $3k. The provider's terms limit using outputs to train competing models. You have 600k historical messages (no labels) and the option of a small open-weights model.
questions.promptHtml: Plan a distillation project and describe how you would de-risk it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Fine-tune a small model on the large model's outputs" with no eval design, licence check or fallback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the provider's licence permit this use (check with legal first)? Latency target? Label distribution and rare classes? Compliance needs for data handling?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; secure licensing clarity before collecting data.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a small model matches on common intents; (b) rare classes and odd phrasing are weaker; (c) drift as products change; (d) labels from the teacher contain errors.
  4. How I'd verify each: Keep the 3,000 labeled set strictly held out; sample 600k messages stratified by intent; compare student to teacher and to human labels per class; measure confidence calibration.
  5. Root cause: Cost is driven by using a general frontier model for a narrow task.
  6. Fix: Label a diverse sample with the permitted teacher (or humans or an open-weights teacher if terms forbid), filter with schema validation and agreement checks, fine-tune the student, deploy with a confidence threshold that routes uncertain messages (for example 10 percent) to the big model. Estimate: 90 percent of traffic at small-model cost plus 10 percent at big-model cost, roughly $2.2k + a small serving cost, within budget if hosting is cheap.
  7. Prevention: Weekly drift monitor on class distribution and confidence; periodic relabel of a sample; retrain cadence; rollback to the teacher.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not evaluate on training prompts; not drop the fallback; not ignore terms of service.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Student reaches 91 percent vs 94? → Inspect per-class gaps; add hard examples; possibly raise the routing share.
  • New label added next month? → Pipeline must support quick relabel and retrain.
  • Latency? → A small model improves latency too, a side benefit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A distilled classifier looked great until a new product launch shifted phrasing; confidence monitoring caught the drift before customers did.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no eval, no fallback.
  • Hire: held-out eval, fallback routing, cost estimate.
  • Strong hire: licence check, stratified sampling, calibration, drift plan and clear cost model.

questions.promptHtml: You prune a model to 2:4 sparsity and quantize it to 4-bit, but decode latency barely improves. Why, and what would you change?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can reason about which bottleneck each technique targets.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: 2:4 sparsity accelerates the matrix multiplication on sparse tensor cores, but decode at small batch is memory-bound, so faster math does not help much; and quantized weights in the sparse format may lack a fused kernel, so you pay extra dequant and index overhead. Quality risk also compounds. I would profile, then keep the optimization that targets the real bottleneck, usually weight quantization for decode, and drop sparsity unless prefill or large batches dominate.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Matmul with sparse tensor cores can reach up to about 2x, but only on compute-bound work. In decode, time is dominated by reading weights. 2:4 storage saves about half the values but adds metadata, so bytes read drop less than 50 percent, and 4-bit with sparsity needs specialized kernels that may not exist in your serving engine.

Check: GPU utilization (compute vs memory), kernel traces, tokens/s versus batch size. Evaluate quality separately for each step, since sparsity plus 4-bit compounds errors; sparse models usually need fine-tuning to recover.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Stacking optimizations without a profile.
  • Measuring speed on prefill and claiming decode gains.
  • Skipping per-step quality evals.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When does 2:4 pay off? → Compute-bound regimes: prefill and large batches on Ampere/Hopper.
  2. Alternatives for decode latency? → Weight quantization, speculative decoding, smaller dense (structured-pruned) model.
  3. Sparse and fp8 together? → Possible on supported hardware; verify engine support and measure.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "should be 2x from sparsity." Senior: maps each technique to the bottleneck and demands a profile.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sparse+int4 build looked 1.9x faster in a matmul microbenchmark but gave 1.1x end to end, since decode was bandwidth-bound and attention was untouched.

questions.contextHtml: An AWQ 4-bit 8B model served on one H100 gave 3x lower latency than bf16 in testing at batch 1 (45 ms to 15 ms per token). After a launch, traffic grows 10x; the server now runs batches of about 96. The 4-bit replica's throughput is only 1.15x the bf16 replica, and GPU utilization is 92 percent. Cost per million tokens barely moved.
questions.promptHtml: Why did the speedup vanish, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Says the quantization is broken or buys more GPUs without understanding the regime change.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which kernel is used? Is KV cache the new memory consumer? Prompt vs output mix? Is the engine up to date for this quant format?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Scale out replicas to protect latency while investigating.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) at batch 96 decode is compute-bound, so weight-only savings shrink while dequantization overhead remains; (b) attention/KV reads now dominate and were never quantized; (c) the weight-only kernel is not optimized for large batches; (d) scheduler/prefill interference, a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: Profile with the engine's metrics and a kernel trace; plot throughput vs batch size for bf16, W4A16 and FP8; check KV memory share.
  5. Root cause: Batch size crossed from the memory-bound to the compute-bound regime, where W4A16 still computes in fp16 and pays dequant cost.
  6. Fix: Switch the throughput tier to FP8 (weights and activations) on H100 so the math itself is faster, add FP8 KV cache, and keep W4A16 for the low-latency tier. Split tiers by traffic profile.
  7. Prevention: Benchmark at the production batch distribution, not just batch 1; keep a capacity curve per precision.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not revert to bf16, which is slower and costlier; run the quality eval again for FP8.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Low-traffic hours? → Batches shrink and W4A16 wins again; route accordingly.
  • Context lengths are 3x longer? → KV cache dominates; quantize KV, consider prefix caching.
  • GPUs are A100? → No FP8; use int8 W8A8 or accept scaling out.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A benchmark at batch 1 chose the wrong precision for a batch-heavy product; the capacity curve fixed the choice in a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames quantization quality or buys GPUs.
  • Hire: identifies compute-bound regime and proposes FP8.
  • Strong hire: tiered serving by traffic profile, KV quantization, capacity curves and re-evaluation.

questions.contextHtml: You will replace a bf16 model with a quantized and partially distilled variant for an assistant serving 5M requests a day. Offline eval shows quality within 1 point and cost down 55 percent. Past experience: offline sets miss tail behaviors. Compliance requires refusal behavior to stay unchanged. You need a rollout plan with a rollback path.
questions.promptHtml: Describe the migration and the guardrails you would put in place.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Deploy to all users since the eval passed."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which metrics define success (task success, refusal rate, latency, user feedback)? Rollback time requirement? Which segments are riskiest (long context, code, languages)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the old model warm and routable for instant rollback.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) tail slices regress (long context, rare languages, structured output); (b) refusal and safety behavior shifts; (c) latency under real batching differs from tests; (d) cost savings smaller than predicted at real traffic mix.
  4. How I'd verify each: Sliced offline eval including long-context recall, tool-call validity, safety red-team set; shadow traffic comparing outputs to the old model; then canary 1, 5, 25, 50, 100 percent with automatic abort thresholds.
  5. Root cause: Not a fault but a risk: averages hide regressions in tails.
  6. Fix (the plan): Shadow mode for a week, canary by cohort, live metrics per slice (task success, refusal rate, tool errors, p95 latency, user thumbs), an LLM-judge plus human sampling on disagreements, abort on any gate breach, a fallback router that sends low-confidence or long-context requests to the old model.
  7. Prevention: Make this the standard gate for every precision or model change; log model version on each request for forensics.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not decommission the old model for at least a full release cycle; not rely on one aggregate score.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Canary shows 0.4 point drop in one language? → Hold at that stage, fix or route that language to the old model.
  • Cost saving appears lower? → Compare token mix and cache hit rates; real prompts may be longer.
  • Refusal rate moved from 2.1 to 2.9 percent? → Block rollout, investigate; compliance gate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A canary at 5 percent caught a rise in malformed tool calls that offline evals missed because the tool schemas in test were simpler than production ones.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: full cutover on offline eval.
  • Hire: canary with metrics and rollback.
  • Strong hire: shadow plus sliced eval, safety gate, fallback routing, automated aborts and model-version logging.
